findings.failure_mode: Tus-Resumable version guard is a no-op, so the protocol-version check never rejects any client
findings.trigger: An attacker sends any arbitrary value in the Tus-Resumable header (e.g. a bogus or future version string) with POST /, HEAD /:uploadId or PATCH /:uploadId; the guard passes and the request reaches the upload handlers as if it were a supported client.
findings.business_impact: Any client, including non-conforming or malicious ones, is accepted by the upload API; version-based protocol assumptions in downstream handlers (offset accounting, extension negotiation) cannot be relied on, affecting all users of the upload service.
attack_chain: All tus routes mounted by lib/tusboy/index.js: POST /, HEAD /:uploadId, PATCH /:uploadId: attacker-controlled input arrives
lib/tusboy/index.js:39 - The version predicate used by the guard is hard-coded to always return true, so no version string is ever rejected.

lib/tusboy/index.js:49-58 - assertTusResumableHeader is applied to every request entering nextRouter, but its only rejection branch depends on versionSupported, which can never fail; only a completely missing header is rejected.
lib/tusboy/index.js:69-73 - The guard is wired in front of all state-changing handlers (post/head/patch), so every one of them trusts that the version was validated when it effectively was not.

Fails here: versionSupported is stubbed to always return true, so the 'Tus-Resumable version not supported' branch in assertTusResumableHeader is unreachable; the router assumes version negotiation happened but it never does.

exploit_path.action: The version predicate used by the guard is hard-coded to always return true, so no version string is ever rejected.

findings.failure_mode: CORS reflects any origin on the upload API while the web client authenticates with a custom x-passwd header
findings.trigger: A malicious web page opened by a user issues fetch()/XHR calls to the tus endpoints (POST / to create uploads, PATCH /:uploadId to write chunks) with the browser automatically attaching the permissive CORS response; because Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoes the attacker's origin, the page can also read responses such as Upload-Offset and Upload-Length.
findings.business_impact: Any website can silently create and modify uploads on the service from a visitor's browser and read upload state, enabling cross-site file injection/abuse against the service and its users; the x-passwd protection only helps if the password is required, and the CORS policy does not restrict who may attempt the API.
findings.blast_radius: Components on the path: lib/tusboy/index.js, app/src/Upload/store/config.js
attack_chain: lib/tusboy/index.js router (POST /, HEAD /:uploadId, PATCH /:uploadId, OPTIONS *) reached cross-origin from any website: attacker-controlled input arrives
lib/tusboy/index.js:60-63 - CORS is configured with origin: true, which reflects any requesting Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and exposes tus protocol headers to the browser.

lib/tusboy/index.js:78-83 - setCorsHeaders is applied to every request before the tus handlers, so cross-origin browser requests from any site are permitted and their responses (including exposed tus headers) are readable by the calling page.

app/src/Upload/store/config.js:24-25 - The legitimate client authenticates to the same API surface using a custom x-passwd header, showing the API is intended to be protected by that secret; a reflected-origin CORS policy lets any third-party page drive the same endpoints from a victim's browser.

Fails here: cors({ origin: true }) reflects every Origin instead of restricting to trusted origins, so the tus upload API is callable and readable cross-origin from any website, with no allowlist anywhere in the shown routing code.

findings.failure_mode: Attacker-controlled upload metadata is forwarded verbatim to the configured webhook endpoint
findings.trigger: An attacker uploads a file via the tus endpoint with arbitrary Upload-Metadata (or an arbitrary filename); when the fileUploaded event fires, the server sends that fully attacker-controlled JSON body to config.fileUploadedWebhook, and on download the file record is sent to config.fileDownloadedWebhook — allowing crafted payloads to be delivered to whatever internal endpoint the webhook targets.
findings.business_impact: Attacker-controlled content is relayed by the server to the webhook destination (potential internal/localhost service), enabling data injection into internal consumers of the webhook and abuse of the server as an outbound request proxy for the metadata it carries; harm falls on the webhook receiver and the service operator.
findings.blast_radius: Components on the path: plugins/file-uploaded-webhook.js, plugins/file-downloaded-webhook.js
attack_chain: tus POST / (upload creation) -> 'fileUploaded' event -> plugins/file-uploaded-webhook.js outbound HTTP POST: attacker-controlled input arrives

plugins/file-uploaded-webhook.js:11-19 - The plugin subscribes to the fileUploaded event and posts the event's metadata field, which originates from the uploader's request, to the configured webhook URL with no validation or sanitisation.
plugins/file-downloaded-webhook.js:12-22 - The sibling plugin does the same for download events, forwarding the whole file record (including attacker-supplied name/metadata) to the configured URL.

Fails here: The webhook plugins assume the event payload is trusted server-side data; nothing validates that metadata/file fields are safe before they are serialised into an outbound HTTP request to a URL that may be an internal service.

findings.failure_mode: Path-jail bypass in Store.getFilename via prefix-confused startsWith check, reachable from both upload and download routes
findings.trigger: 1) Send POST to the files endpoint with Upload-Metadata containing sid = '../<uploadDirName><suffix>' (e.g. '../uploads-backup'); the assert only checks presence, and req.FID becomes '../uploads-backup++<uuid>'. 2) store.getFilename resolves this to '<parent-of-uploadDir>/uploads-backup/<uuid>', which passes the startsWith check, so the uploaded bytes and the .json metadata are written outside the upload jail. 3) The same bypass works for reads: GET /files/..++<uploadDirName><suffix> resolves to a sibling path that passes the prefix check, and store.info()/res.download() serve it (info requires a matching '.json' sidecar, which the write path above creates).
findings.business_impact: Arbitrary file write (attacker-controlled content plus a JSON sidecar) and read of any path on the filesystem whose absolute path begins with the configured uploadDir string, e.g. sibling directories like '<uploadDir>-backup' or files such as '<uploadDir>base.json'. This can overwrite application data/config sidecars and exfiltrate files outside the upload jail; harm falls on the server operator and on users whose files are stored next to the upload directory.
findings.blast_radius: Components on the path: lib/endpoints.js, lib/store.js
attack_chain: POST {uploadAppPath}files (Upload-Metadata header controls sid) and GET {baseUrl}files/:fid (URL param controls fid): attacker-controlled input arrives

lib/endpoints.js:196-246 - Upload middleware decodes attacker-controlled Upload-Metadata and only asserts that sid is present (no charset/format validation); it then builds the storage key as meta.sid + '++' + meta.key and hands it to tusboy via req.FID.
lib/endpoints.js:285-286 - The single-file download route passes the raw URL parameter straight into the store with no validation of its shape or membership in a known bucket.

lib/store.js:29-35 - getFilename converts the first '++' to '/' and resolves against the upload dir, then 'jails' the result with a string-prefix check that does not require a path-separator boundary.

lib/store.js:40-43 - create()/update()/append() all write through getFilename, so an upload whose sid escapes the jail prefix is persisted outside the intended directory (both the data file and its .json sidecar).

Fails here: The jail check `p.startsWith(this.dir)` compares a resolved absolute path against the upload-dir string without a trailing path separator, so any sibling path whose name merely begins with the upload-dir name (e.g. dir '/srv/uploads' vs '/srv/uploadsX/...') is accepted. Additionally, only the first '++' is replaced, and neither the upload middleware nor the download route validates the sid/fid format before it reaches the store.

exploit_path.action: Upload middleware decodes attacker-controlled Upload-Metadata and only asserts that sid is present (no charset/format validation); it then builds the storage key as meta.sid + '++' + meta.key and hands it to tusboy via req.FID.
The single-file download route passes the raw URL parameter straight into the store with no validation of its shape or membership in a known bucket.

    res.download(store.getFilename(req.params.fid), info.metadata.name);

findings.failure_mode: Bucket download password enforced only on the listing route, bypassed by direct file and archive download URLs
findings.trigger: An attacker who obtains any single file URL (sid++uuid key) or the archive link — e.g. from the fileUploaded/fileDownloaded webhook plugins (plugins/file-uploaded-webhook.js, plugins/file-downloaded-webhook.js emit the URL), server logs, browser history, or a referrer — can GET /files/<sid>++<key> directly and receive the file with no password prompt, even though the bucket is password-protected and the listing endpoint correctly returns 401.
findings.business_impact: Complete bypass of per-bucket download passwords; all files in a protected bucket (including archives of the whole bucket) are readable by anyone holding or leaking a file URL. Harms every uploader who relied on the password option.
attack_chain: GET {baseUrl}files/:fid (single file) and GET {baseUrl}files/:fid.tar.gz|.zip (archive): attacker-controlled input arrives

lib/endpoints.js:170-173 - The bucket listing route is the ONLY place a per-bucket download password is checked: it compares the x-download-pass header against item.metadata.password before returning item URLs.

lib/endpoints.js:285-286 - The direct download route takes req.params.fid (sid++key), calls store.info() and res.download() with no x-download-pass check and no db lookup of the bucket password. The guard defined in the sibling route is never applied here.

lib/endpoints.js:archive branch of the same /files/:fid route - The tar.gz/zip archive download validates only that the filename matches MD5(bucket keys), never the bucket password, then streams every file in the bucket.

Fails here: The password check for password-protected buckets exists only in the `/:sid.json` listing handler; the `/files/:fid` handlers assume the unguessable URL is itself the secret and never re-validate x-download-pass against db metadata.
